Deformation and Velocity Gradient Tensor

Tobias Stephan

2026-10-30

Source: vignettes/deformation.qmd

This tutorial demonstrates how {structr} can be used to deform orientation data using deformation and velocity gradient tensors. This can be useful to simulate progressive deformation and change of orientation. It will also demonstrate how you can combine different deformation tensors, and how to extract other flow parameters (such as vorticity, stretching, and dilatation).

library(structr)

Deformation gradient tensor

The 3D deformation gradient tensor F is a matrix that linearly transforms points. In other words, it describes how the positions of points change in three dimensions during homogeneous deformation.

Define a deformation gradient tensor

The deformation matrix can be defined in several ways:

  • defgrad_by_comp() creates a tensor defined by its individual components (default is the identity tensor).
  • defgrad_by_ratio() creates an isochoric tensor with axial stretches defined by strain ratios (default is the identity tensor).
  • defgrad_from_vectors() creates a tensor representing a rotation around the axis perpendicular to both vectors, rotating v1 to v2.
  • defgrad_from_axisangle() creates a tensor representing a rigid-body rotation about an axis by an angle.
  • defgrad_from_pureshear() creates an isochoric coaxial tensor.
  • defgrad_from_simpleshear() creates an isochoric non-coaxial tensor.
  • defgrad_from_generalshear() creates an isochoric tensor, where transtension is k>1k>1 and γ≠0\gamma \neq 0, and transpression is k<1k<1 and γ≠0\gamma \neq 0 (Sanderson & Marchini, 19841; Fossen & Tikoff, 19932).
  • defgrad_from_dilation() creates a tensor representing volume change in the z-direction.
D1 <- defgrad_from_generalshear(k = 2.5, gamma = 0.9)
print(D1)
#> Deformation gradient tensor
#>      [,1]     [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1 1.473332  0.0
#> [2,]    0 2.500000  0.0
#> [3,]    0 0.000000  0.4

Matrix algebra

An isochoric deformation tensor creates deformation without volume change. In that case, the determinant of the matrix must be 1. In R, this can be checked using det():

det(D1)
#> [1] 1

The inverse of the tensor reverses the deformation. In R, this can be done using solve():

solve(D1)
#>      [,1]       [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1 -0.5893326  0.0
#> [2,]    0  0.4000000  0.0
#> [3,]    0  0.0000000  2.5

The eigenvectors of F itself are the material lines that are not rotated by the deformation (the finite apophyses). Only for coaxial deformation (symmetric F) do they coincide with the principal axes of the strain ellipsoid.

eigen(D1)
#> eigen() decomposition
#> $values
#> [1] 2.5 1.0 0.4
#> 
#> $vectors
#>           [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,] 0.7007364    1    0
#> [2,] 0.7134203    0    0
#> [3,] 0.0000000    0    1

The orientation and shape of the strain ellipsoid are given by the left Cauchy–Green tensor 𝑩=𝑭𝑭⊤\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{F}\mathbf{F}^\top: its eigenvectors are the principal strain axes, and the square roots of its eigenvalues λ\lambda are the principal stretches (i.e. the lengths of the ellipsoid axes):

B_eig <- eigen(D1 %*% t(D1))
B_eig$vectors
#>           [,1]       [,2] [,3]
#> [1,] 0.5542262  0.8323661    0
#> [2,] 0.8323661 -0.5542262    0
#> [3,] 0.0000000  0.0000000    1
sqrt(B_eig$values)
#> [1] 2.9500039 0.8474565 0.4000000

Deformation tensors can be combined using matrix multiplication. The resulting deformation from our general-shear deformation (D1) superimposed by our rotation (D2) is

D2 <- defgrad_from_axisangle(Line(0, 90), 30)

D12 <- D2 %*% D1 # D1 is applied first

Caution

Matrix multiplication is not commutative, i.e. in general 𝑫𝟏⋅𝑫𝟐≠𝑫𝟐⋅𝑫𝟏\mathbf{D_1} \cdot \mathbf{D_2} \neq \mathbf{D_2} \cdot \mathbf{D_1}.

Transformation using deformation gradient tensor

The deformation can now be applied on some orientation data using linear transformation:

# generate some random lineation
xl <- rvmf(100, mu = Line(0, 90), k = 100)

xl_transformed <- transform_linear(xl, D1)
head(xl_transformed)
#> Vector (Vec3) object (n = 6):
#>                x           y         z
#> [1,]  0.14739869  0.06221709 0.3974155
#> [2,]  0.34631353  0.18893690 0.3876244
#> [3,] -0.26872762 -0.29431706 0.3953859
#> [4,]  0.04479873  0.03775757 0.3998527
#> [5,]  0.10463240  0.14584865 0.3992488
#> [6,] -0.23724406 -0.26484370 0.3964220

Let’s visualize the deformation:

# The coordinate axes of our deformation tensor:
axes <- Vec3(c(1, 0, 0), c(0, 1, 0), c(0, 0, 1))

stereoplot(guides = FALSE) # turn off guidelines for better visibility
points(xl, col = "grey", pch = 16)
points(xl_transformed, col = "#B63679FF", pch = 16)
points(axes, pch = 15)
text(axes, labels = c("x", "y", "z"), pos = 1, font = 3)

legend("right", legend = c("D0", "D1"), col = c("grey", "#B63679FF"), pch = 16)

Velocity gradient tensor

The velocity gradient tensor L describes the velocity of particles at any instant during the deformation. It can be derived from a deformation gradient tensor:

  • The time argument specifies the duration over which the finite deformation F accumulates, so that steady flow with velocity gradient L for this time produces F.
L <- velgrad(D1, time = 10)

Decomposition

The velocity gradient tensor L can be decomposed into a symmetric matrix S (the strain rate or stretching tensor) and a skew-symmetric matrix W (the spin tensor).

The stretching tensor describes the portion of the deformation that over time produces strain:

S <- velgrad_rate(L)

The spin tensor contains information about the internal rotation during the deformation:

W <- velgrad_spin(L)

The eigenvectors of the stretching tensor give the orientations of the instantaneous stretching axes, and its eigenvalues the instantaneous stretching rates:

S_eig <- eigen(S)

# ISA vectors (eigenvectors are the columns, hence the transpose)
axes_ISA <- S_eig$vectors |>
  t() |>
  as.Vec3() |>
  Line()

# Stretching rates
S_eig$values
#> [1]  0.11003269 -0.01840362 -0.09162907

Tip

The shortcut functions instantaneous_stretching_axes(L) and instantaneous_stretching(L) produce the same results as above.

The eigenvectors of the velocity gradient tensor describe the flow apophyses:

L_eig <- eigen(L)

# Flow apophyses
flow_vectors <- L_eig$vectors |>
  t() |>
  as.Vec3()

flow_apophyses <- rbind(
  crossprod(flow_vectors[1, ], flow_vectors[2, ]),
  crossprod(flow_vectors[2, ], flow_vectors[3, ])
) |> Plane()

Tip

Shortcut: flow_apophyses(L)

The angle α between the apophyses is directly related to how close to simple shear or pure shear the deformation is. α is zero for simple shear and 90° for pure shear. The kinematic vorticity number WkW_k is given by Wk=cos⁡αW_k = \cos\alpha:

alpha <- angle(flow_apophyses[1, ], flow_apophyses[2, ])
abs(cos(alpha * pi / 180))
#> [1] 0.7007364

Tip

Shortcut: kinematic_vorticity_from_velgrad(L)

The vorticity vector is the axial vector of the spin tensor W. For monoclinic flows such as this one, it is parallel to the eigenvector of L that is common to both flow apophysis planes:

Line(flow_vectors[2, ])
#> Line object (n = 1):
#> azimuth  plunge 
#>       0      90

# cross-check: axial vector of W
Line(Vec3(W[3, 2], W[1, 3], W[2, 1]))
#> Line object (n = 1):
#> azimuth  plunge 
#>     180      90

Tip

Shortcut: vorticity_vector(L)

Strain increments

Now we can extract the deformation gradient tensor accumulated after a given time. Here we extract the deformation gradient tensors for some time steps using defgrad():

  • The steps argument specifies how many increments you would like to extract (this is also the “resolution” of the deformation path).
  • The time argument is the total duration of the deformation.
D1_steps <- defgrad(L, time = 10, steps = 2)

Now apply the deformation tensors on some orientation data:

xl_steps <- lapply(D1_steps, function(i) {
  transform_linear(xl, i)
})

Visualization of deformation over time

And plot the paths showing how the orientations change over time:

increments <- seq(0, 10, 2)
cols <- assign_col(increments)

stereoplot(guides = FALSE) # turn off guidelines for better visibility

# plot the strain increments
stereo_path(xl_steps, type = "l")
stereo_path(xl_steps, type = "p", col = cols, pch = 16, cex = .4)

# flow apophyses
lines(flow_apophyses, col = c("grey30", "grey70"), lty = c(1, 2))

# instantaneous stretching axes
points(axes_ISA, pch = 15, col = "#B63679FF")
text(axes_ISA, labels = c("ISA-1", "ISA-2", "ISA-3"), col = "#B63679FF", pos = 3, font = 2)

# coordinate axes of def-tensor
points(axes, pch = 15)
text(axes, labels = c("x", "y", "z"), pos = 1, font = 3)

# legend
legend(0, -1.1,
  xjust = 0.5,
  legend = c("Flow apophysis 1", "Flow apophysis 2"),
  col = c("grey30", "grey70"),
  lty = c(1, 2)
)
legend_col(increments, title = "Time")

We can also monitor how the orientation tensor changes during progressive deformation:

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
vollmer_plot(xl_steps, type = "b", col = cols)
hsu_plot(xl_steps, type = "b", col = cols)
